Raphael, Raffaello Sanzio, from 1483 to 1520, was an Italian Renaissance master painter and architect whose harmonious compositions, graceful figures, and mastery of perspective and color made him one of the three greatest figures of the High Renaissance, alongside Leonardo da Vinci and Michelangelo. Working primarily in Rome under papal patronage, Raphael decorated the Vatican Palace with frescoes including the iconic School of Athens, revolutionized portrait painting, and demonstrated that emotional and intellectual depth could be achieved through clarity and balance rather than Leonardo's sfumato or Michelangelo's dramatic power.

Raphael was born in Urbino, a center of Renaissance learning. His father was a painter and court official, and Raphael trained under Perugino, absorbing the Umbrian school's emphasis on clear forms and serene composition. Pope Julius II hired Raphael in 1508 to decorate the papal apartments, the Stanze di Raffaello, in the Vatican. Over the next twelve years, Raphael and his workshop painted vast frescoes covering the walls and ceilings, the most famous being the School of Athens.

The School of Athens, painted in 1511, depicts Plato and Aristotle at the center of a gathering of ancient philosophers arranged in perfect geometric harmony. The fresco showcases Raphael's mastery of linear perspective, foreshortening, and psychological portraiture. Each philosopher has a distinct, believable character. Raphael's approach balanced Leonardo's empirical precision and sfumato with Michelangelo's sculptural musculature and dramatic energy. His style favored clarity, symmetry, and grace, a synthesis rather than an idiosyncratic genius.

He revolutionized portrait painting, creating dignified, psychologically penetrating likenesses that influenced portraiture for centuries. His Portrait of a Young Woman, often called La Fornarina, is celebrated for its delicate rendering and human presence. Raphael was also an architect. He redesigned the facade of the Palazzo Madama, served as architect of Saint Peter's Basilica after Donato Bramante's death, and planned urban spaces in Rome. His architectural vision emphasized classical proportion and harmony.

Raphael died unexpectedly at age 37, likely from a fever. His early death ended a career that, though brief, had already established him as Christendom's leading artistic authority. His pupils and followers spread his influence across Europe for generations. Raphael's workshop, called the bottega, was enormous and highly organized. His ability to delegate while maintaining a unified aesthetic made him prolific. He managed multiple major commissions simultaneously while training dozens of assistants, establishing the model of the Renaissance workshop as a creative factory.
